choices.text: Hand over the Sealed Satchel
Refuse — the satchel is going to its intended recipient
Ask what is inside the satchel

sections.narrative:
You set the Sealed Satchel on the cedar table.

The Spymaster does not open it immediately. They simply place one hand on it, the way a person touches something they have been waiting a long time to hold.

"Good," they say. "You'll leave by the river gate tonight. There is a boat. Don't ask where it goes — that is not your concern any longer."

You are given a name. A coin. A cloak that isn't yours.

You never learn what was in the satchel. Years later you will hear rumours — a treaty, a succession document, a list of names — but the truth of it has gone wherever the Spymaster sends things that must not exist. You survived the Iron Road. That is enough.

You never looked back.

You leave the arcade without the satchel changing hands. The Spymaster does not follow you — they are not that kind of operator. But you have made your position clear: you are not selling.

The market churns around you. The Lord's Agent is still out there. The palace district entrance is still across the city. The docks are south.

choices.text: Try the palace district
Go to the docks
Reconsider — go back to the Spymaster
Look for the Lord's Agent in the textile quarter

sections.narrative:
The docks run along the river that backs the palace district — a working waterfront of grain barges, fishing skiffs, and the occasional unmarked cutter whose cargo never appears in any manifest. It is loud, smelly, and thoroughly overlooked by the kind of authority that watches the main roads.

The spy ring has a contact here — or had one, before the assassins started cleaning up. At the far end of the dockside, beyond the grain warehouses, a set of old stone steps leads down to a private pontoon from which you can see the palace district walls reflected in the brown river water.

An iron brazier sits beside the steps, filled with old rope and dry wood. Unlit.

You think about the satchel. About what it would mean to light that fire.

choices.text: Look for the spy ring contact
Light the brazier and burn the satchel
Use the river approach to reach the palace district
Head back to the market district

sections.narrative:
You hold the satchel over the brazier. The wax seal catches first, running liquid down the leather like dark tears, and then the leather itself begins to brown at the edges. You think of the courier on the road, of the men who killed him, of every faction that has been moving pieces across this board without your consent.

The satchel catches.

Whatever was inside it — treaty, list, evidence, or nothing — is smoke now. The fire is brief and total. You watch it until there is nothing left but ash and a twisted metal clasp.

Are you certain?

choices.text: Let it burn — you are certain
Pull it back — there is still time

sections.narrative:
The ash falls into the river.

You stand by the brazier for a long time, watching the current take it. The palace district lights are coming on across the water. Somewhere in the city, factions are waiting for word of a satchel that no longer exists.

They will wait a long time.

You walk back along the dockside. Nobody stops you. Nobody is watching a person with nothing to carry. The Iron Road brought you here — courier, courier's killer, spy, and a hundred other titles you never wanted — and now it ends in ash and the smell of the river.

You are no one. You are free.

Three kingdoms will arrange themselves without the contents of that satchel. Whether that is better or worse, you find you do not particularly care.

The palace district begins where the main city ends: a gatehouse checkpoint staffed by royal household guards in formal livery, not the city's watch. The arch behind them is narrower than the city gate, older stone, and the guards carry halberds rather than pikes.

Access to the palace district is not negotiable through coin — the household guards are differently corrupt, beholden to a different master. What they respect is credentials: the bronze of a Courier's Token, the specific cut of a Relay Station Key on its cord, or a Spymaster's Letter in the right sealed format.

Without one of these, the only way in is the river approach or a significant piece of luck.

choices.text: Present your Courier's Token at the checkpoint
Present your Relay Station Key at the checkpoint
Show the Spymaster's Letter — you have a prearranged contact inside
Try the river approach from the docks
You have no credentials — you need another route

sections.narrative:
The river approach is the route the palace district's servants and suppliers use when the main gate is closed: a series of stone steps cut into the embankment, leading to a low postern gate that is locked but not guarded at this hour.

You came prepared — or you make do with what you have. The gate is old iron, the lock a simple design. If you know such things, it is perhaps two minutes' work. If you do not, it is considerably longer, and the barge traffic on the river means you are not entirely unobserved.

The lock clicks. You are through.

choices.text: Move quickly — find the palace anteroom

sections.narrative:
The spy ring contact is where they were supposed to be — a grey-haired woman mending nets at the end of the third dock, who looks at you with the flat recognition of someone who expected you two days ago.

"You're late," she says. "The Contact has been moved. The palace anteroom, not the relay station. If you're delivering, go to the anteroom. If you're not delivering, I can't help you."

She adds, after a pause: "The Lord's Agent has people at the main gate. Use the river steps if you're going in."

She goes back to her nets.

choices.text: Take the river steps to the palace district
You're not delivering — burn the satchel instead
Head for the main palace gate regardless

sections.narrative:
The Lord's Agent finds you before you find them — or it is the other way round, and the distinction no longer matters. They are sitting at a table in a covered part of the market with a cup of something warm and a view of every entrance.

They look exactly as they did at the Crossroads Inn: polished, unhurried, dangerous in the specific way that people are dangerous when they can afford to wait.

"I thought you might come," they say. "Sit down. I have a proposition that doesn't require you to trust anyone you've met on this road."

They place a leather wallet on the table between you. It is thick with coin.

choices.text: Hear the offer
Walk away — you have not come this far to sell

sections.narrative:
"Two hundred gold," the Lord's Agent says. "That is more than a courier earns in five years. More than most people earn in a life. You hand me the satchel under this table, we both stand up and walk in opposite directions, and this is over."

They add: "The alternative is that I wait until the palace guards catch you — and they will, at your suspicion level — and collect it for nothing. I'm being generous. It won't last."

They slide the wallet half an inch closer.

You look at the wallet. You look at the satchel. You think about the courier on the road.

choices.text: Take the coin — hand over the Sealed Satchel
Refuse — stand up and leave
Refuse and draw the Assassin's Blade

sections.narrative:
You take the coin. The satchel changes hands under the table, smooth as any market transaction. The Lord's Agent does not smile — they simply pocket the satchel, stand, and straighten their coat.

"Pleasure," they say.

Then they are gone.

You sit with the wallet for a moment. Two hundred gold. It is, as advertised, a great deal of money. It is also, as advertised, the end of this.

You never know what was in the satchel. You suspect you are better off not knowing. The Lord who sent those killers on the Iron Road will have what they wanted; the courier who died for it will remain unavenged; the three kingdoms will continue their arrangements without your interference.

You leave the market. You buy passage on the first coach leaving the city. The Iron Road brought you here. Another road will take you somewhere else.

You are, against considerable odds, alive.

You stand. The Lord's Agent watches you with the same patient expression, neither surprised nor offended.

"Your choice," they say. "I'll be here when you change your mind."

You do not change your mind. You walk out of the textile quarter and into the wider market, the satchel still with you, the coin wallet still on their table.

The palace district is across the city. The docks are south. The Spymaster is still in the south arcade. Whatever you decide, you are going to have to decide it soon — the afternoon is failing and you cannot stay in this city much longer.

choices.text: Go to the palace district
Find the Spymaster
Head for the docks

sections.narrative:
The blade comes out. The Lord's Agent's eyes widen — not with fear, with something colder.

They are fast. You are faster, or you are not.

scripts.onCombatEnd: if ctx.getStat('STAMINA') > 0 then ctx.navigateTo(168) else ctx.navigateTo(167) end

choices.text: Flee — sheathe the blade and run before it goes further

sections.narrative:
You run. The Lord's Agent does not give immediate chase — too public, too much noise already from the fight — but you hear shouting behind you, the scramble of boots on cobblestones, and you know the market's quiet tolerance has a limit.

You take a lane, then another, and come out somewhere on the market's north edge, breathing hard. Nobody is following. The city continues indifferently around you.

choices.text: Get clear of the market — go to the docks
Push on to the palace district while you still can

sections.narrative:
You hold up the Courier's Token — the bronze disc bearing the royal courier corps insignia. The household guard examines it without touching it, then looks at you for a long moment, measuring.

"Courier's business," he says finally. It is not a question.

"Courier's business," you agree.

He stands aside. You walk through the arch into the palace district.

choices.text: Proceed to the palace anteroom

sections.narrative:
The Relay Station Key has the same effect as credentials should have: immediate, definite, and wordless. The household guard examines the cut of the key, checks it against something in a pocket register, and opens the smaller gate to the right of the main arch.

"Relay courier route," he says. "Anteroom is through the courtyard, second archway on your left."

You are inside the palace district.

choices.text: Follow his directions to the anteroom

sections.narrative:
The palace district is quieter than the city outside it — less crowd, more guard, less noise of commerce and more the particular hush of power operating at a remove from the people it governs. The courtyard is swept stone, the buildings around it faced with carved marble.

The anteroom is a narrow hall off the main courtyard — not grand, which surprises you. An office, almost. A place where things arrive and are recorded and passed upward.

There is someone waiting.

scripts.onEnter: if state.get('contactAlive') then ctx.navigateTo(158) else ctx.navigateTo(160) end

sections.narrative:
The Courier's Contact is an elderly person of indeterminate rank, dressed in the quiet grey of a senior official, who rises when you enter with a speed that belies their age.

They look at you, then at the satchel — if you carry it.

"You are not the courier," they say. It is not an accusation.

"No," you say.

"But you have come. And the satchel is…" They pause. "Intact?"

You tell them what happened on the Iron Road. What you carried since then. All of it.

They listen without interrupting.

choices.text: Hand over the Sealed Satchel
Tell them the satchel no longer exists

sections.narrative:
You place the Sealed Satchel on the table between you.

The Contact's hands, steadier than they have any right to be, break the wax seal and open the satchel. They read what is inside in silence. You watch their face for a reaction — relief, horror, satisfaction — and receive only a slow exhale.

"This is what we needed," they say. "This is what the courier died for."

They look up at you. "You are owed a great deal. A name, to begin with — yours has been flagged in four jurisdictions since Varenmark. We can clear that. We can do more than that."

What was in the satchel, you eventually learn, was a set of sworn depositions — testimony from border officials about the Lord's assassination contracts, sufficient to bring charges, insufficient alone to convict but enough to make the Lord's position untenable. The courier was killed to stop them. You were not.

In the weeks that follow, a lord retires from public life with quiet speed. A series of officials are dismissed. The border city of Varenmark acquires a new Customs House captain.

Your name is cleared. Your debt — to the road, to the satchel, to the courier you never knew — is paid.

The Contact is not there.

In their place is a younger official — precise, contained, with the watchful affect of someone who has been briefed on a situation and finds it unpleasant.

"The Contact was relocated three days ago," he says. "I have authority to receive the delivery in their stead. I am told to expect a satchel."

He looks at your hands.

He does not offer his name.

choices.text: Hand over the Sealed Satchel to the intelligence officer
Tell him the satchel no longer exists
Say nothing and leave — something is wrong

sections.narrative:
You hand over the satchel.

The officer takes it without ceremony, breaks the seal, reads it, and folds it closed again.

"This is actionable," he says, which tells you nothing. He produces a folded paper — a document, already prepared. "Your name has been cleared of all frontier irregularities. This is a travel pass, valid for any road in the three kingdoms for one year."

He stands, moves to the door, opens it. The audience is over.

You take the travel pass. You walk out of the anteroom into the courtyard, into the pale late light, with nothing in your hands but paper that says you are a free person on a legal road.

Somewhere in the city, the Lord's Agent is still waiting at their table.

Somewhere on the Iron Road, there is a stone where a courier fell.

You begin to walk.

The anteroom door is still open behind you. You step into the courtyard and move quickly — not running, but walking with intention through the second arch and into a service passage that smells of horses.

The officer's voice carries from the anteroom: "Detain them."

There are guards between you and every gate. The palace district, sealed and quiet, has become a trap.

You have seconds to decide.

choices.text: Fight through the palace guards
Go back — surrender the satchel on your terms

sections.narrative:
The palace guards are not the city watch. They are armed, trained, and they have reinforcements behind every arch.

You make it across the courtyard. Not further.

The satchel is taken. You are taken. The depositions inside it are sufficient to clear the official who sent the courier, but your name does not appear in any subsequent proceedings — you are a complication, and complications disappear into the palace district's administrative silence.

No notice is posted. You are simply gone.

The Iron Road continues without you.

The Spymaster's Letter, presented to a particular household guard at a postern gate on the palace district's east wall, produces a result you did not quite expect: the guard reads it, folds it, pockets it, and says, "This way."

You follow him through a succession of corridors that feel like they belong to a different building entirely — lower ceilings, older stone — to a door that opens onto the palace anteroom from the inside.

The route was pre-arranged. The Spymaster has long hands.

choices.text: Enter the anteroom

sections.narrative:
Your hand goes back into the brazier. The leather is hot but not yet gone — you pull the satchel free, slapping out the flames against the stone of the dock, and clutch it to your chest.

The wax seal is destroyed. The satchel's flap has been damaged but the contents — whatever they are — may still be intact.

You breathe. The satchel is still yours. The question of what to do with it has not been answered, only deferred.

choices.text: Go to the palace district and deliver what remains
Find the Spymaster and sell it
Let it go — put it back in the fire

sections.narrative:
You have been standing still for too long in the wrong part of the market.

The plain-coated men arrive in pairs — four of them, closing the angles. No warrants this time. They do not need warrants at this stage. Your suspicion profile in the capital's intelligence network has reached the level where they collect first and document after.

You do not resist. It would not help. The satchel is taken. You are taken to a room that is not a cell but functions like one.

Three days later you are still there. You will remain there for a considerable time.

The Iron Road ends here, without ceremony, in a room with no windows.

The Lord's Agent is fast and thoroughly trained and has, you realise too late, backup two tables away.

The fight in the market is brief. You lose.

You wake in a cellar somewhere in the capital's commercial district. The satchel is gone. So is your coin. Your Assassin's Blade has been kept, presumably as a joke.

The Lord's Agent does not return. Whatever was in the satchel serves its purpose. The Lord it served makes no difficulty about one inconvenient traveller who tried to be a hero.

You are released after two weeks with a warning and a headache.

You never learn what was in the satchel. You never carry anything more dangerous than bread on any road, ever again.

The Lord's Agent goes down hard and stays down. Their backup — you count two, coming fast — sees the result and recalculates. One of them runs. The other holds his position long enough to be brave and then follows.

You stand over the Agent, breathing, and consider your options. They are alive — you are not an assassin. The satchel is still yours.

The market is beginning to notice. You have perhaps two minutes before the city watch arrives.

The Spymaster considers the question.

"Depositions," they say finally. "Sworn testimony. If it reaches royal intelligence it threatens a lord with significant influence. If it reaches me…" They tilt their head. "It becomes a different kind of leverage. Neither outcome is without consequence for the people involved."

They let that settle.

"The question is not what is inside the satchel. The question is whose hands it ends in. That is the only question that has ever mattered on this road."

They wait for your answer.

choices.text: Give the satchel to the Spymaster
No — take it to the palace district

sections.narrative:
You tell them the satchel is gone — burned, sold, or gone by whatever route you chose.

There is a silence.

The Contact, or the officer, absorbs this. Whatever they were expecting, it was not this. The depositions, the testimony, the case against the Lord — it is all smoke now, or in someone else's hands.

"Then there is nothing left to receive," the Contact says quietly.

They do not stop you leaving. There is nothing to stop you for.

You walk out of the palace district through the main gate — your suspicion, whatever it was, irrelevant now that there is nothing to find on you — into the city, onto the road, and you keep walking until the capital is behind you and the Iron Road is just a road again.
